div.p: Existing works on gang task scheduling mainly focus on the preemptive scheduling case, which contradicts a bit with the non-preemptive executing nature of applying gang scheduling techniques in practice. In this paper, we present a set of non-trivial techniques that can analyze the schedulability of scheduling a hard real-time sporadic gang task system under non-preemptive GEDF on multiprocessors and a utilization-based schedulability test (first-of-its-kind) is derived.
512 2019 IEEE Real-Time Systems Symposium (RTSS)

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Although recent techniques for supporting real-time gang tasks on multiprocessors have been shown to be promising [1], they all focus on the preemptive case. This unfortunately contradicts a bit with the motivation and the application scenario of applying gang scheduling in practice. Specifically, gang-based execution on accelerators (e.g., GPU) or shared resources such as memory is typically nonpreemptive. Moreover, allowing gang-grouped threads to be preempted at runtime may incur significant overhead, which may actually negate the parallelism-induced benefits due to gang-base execution. Thus, scheduling gang tasks on multiprocessors in a non-preemptive manner is critical in ensuring realistic implementation in practice.

Unfortunately, combining non-preemptivity with ganginduced parallelism in the hard real-time (HRT) scheduling context raises significant challenges. Consider an intuitive example, where three non-preemptive gang tasks (τ 1 , τ 2 and τ 3 ) are scheduled on four processors under global earliestdeadline-first (GEDF). The degree of parallelism for both τ 1 and τ 2 is 2 while the degree of parallelism of τ 3 is 3. As seen in Fig. 1, at the time instant 5, although there are two idle processors, the scheduler cannot schedule τ 3,1 due to two kinds of blocking: (i) priority-inversion blocking, where τ 3,1 cannot preempt a lower priority job τ 1,1 which is executing at time 5, and (ii) parallelism-induced blocking, where the degree of parallelism of τ 3 is 3, which is larger than the number of idle processors at time 5. For the same reason, τ 3,1 cannot execute till time 35. This example intuitively reveal a fundamental challenge for scheduling and analyzing gang tasks under non- preemptive scheduling, i.e., 2-dimension blocking (2D blocking). This 2D blocking property may incur significant pessimism in analyzing the schedulability of gang tasks. Unlike non-preemptive scheduling of ordinary sporadic tasks where a higher priority job can be blocked by a lower priority job by at most once, a job released by a gang task may be blocked by multiple lower priority jobs (τ 3,1 in the above example is blocked by two jobs). In the worst case, a gang job may experience infinite blocking due to the 2D blocking effect as we shall discuss in detail in Sec. 3. Intuitively, such a worst case scenario may happen if a higher priority gang job can neither preempt an executing job nor execute on idle processors in parallel due to a large degree of parallelism, while lower priority jobs from other tasks may be continuously released and executed on idle processors, causing the number of idle processors to be smaller than the degree of parallelism of the high priority job at any time instant.

To resolve this challenge, this paper aims at developing techniques that can characterize 2D blocking-induced utilization loss for any HRT sporadic gang task system scheduled under non-preemptive GEDF, and derive a corresponding utilization-based schedulability test that is nontrivial. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first utilization-based schedulability test derived for non-preemptively scheduled gang task systems.

div.head: System Model
div.p: We consider the problem of scheduling a set τ = {τ 1 , ..., τ n } of n independent non-preemptive gang tasks on M ≥ 1 identical processors M 1 , M 2 , ..., M m . Note that the number of processors simultaneously used by a sporadic gang task (also called a gang task s degree of parallelism) can be greater than 1, which is an essential difference between a sporadic gang task and an ordinary sporadic task. Each task is released sporadically, with each such invocation called a job. Successive jobs of the same task are required to execute in sequence. We assume that each job of τ i executes for at most e i time units. The j th job of τ i , denoted τ i,j , is released at time instant r i,j and has a deadline at time instant d i,j . Associated with each task τ i are a period p i , which specifies the minimum time between two consecutive job releases of τ i , and a deadline d i , which specifies the relative deadline of each such job, i.e., d i,j = r i,j + d i . Each job of τ i reserves m i processors for at most e i time units. The execution demand of a job of τ i can be represented as an m i × e i rectangle in the time and processor space. Note that a released gang job τ i,j can start execution only if the number of idle processors is at least m i . Thus, an HRT gang task τ i can be characterized by a 4-tuple of parameters -τ i (e i , m i , p i , d i ). The utilization of a task τ i is defined as u i = ei×mi pi , and the utilization of the task system τ as U sum = τi∈τ u i . An task system τ is said to be an implicit-deadline system if d i = p i holds for each τ i . In this paper, we focus on the implicit-deadline task systems.

Throughout the paper, we assume that time is integral, and for any task τ i ∈ τ , each of e i ≥ 1, p i ≥ 1, and d i ≥ 1 is a non-negative integer. Thus, a job that executes at time instant t executes during the entire time interval [t, t + 1). Under non-preemptive Global Early-Deadline-First (GEDF) scheduling algorithm, released jobs are prioritized by their absolute deadlines. We assume that ties are resolved arbitrarily. A job cannot be preempted once it starts execution.

div.head: A Fundamental Challenge: 2D Blocking
div.p: Before presenting our developed analysis techniques in detail, we first intuitively motivate and explain a significant and fundamental challenge due to the combination of nonpreemptive scheduling and gang-induced parallelism.

Example 1. Consider a four-processor sporadic gang task set τ that consists of 7 gang tasks scheduler under nonpreemptive GEDF: τ 1 (2, 2, 14, 14), τ 2 (3, 2, 13, 13), τ 3 (3, 2, 12, 12), τ 4 (3, 2, 10, 10), τ 5 (3, 2, 9, 9), τ 6 (3, 2, 7, 7) and τ 7 (2, 3, 12, 12). Suppose τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 , τ 4 , τ 5 , and τ 6 release only the first job at time instants 0, 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, respectively. τ 7 releases a first job at time instant 1. Clearly, τ 7,1 has the highest priority among all seven first jobs since it has the earliest absolute deadline at 13. However, as seen in Fig. 2,τ 7,1 misses its deadline. Interestingly, for this example, τ 7,1 is actually PIblocked for six times by the other six first jobs. The reason is because at any time instant during [0, 12), the number of idle processor is always less than 3, which allows one of the six jobs to start execution in a non-preemptive manner.

2D blocking as the fundamental challenge. From above example, it is evident that a gang job may suffer 2dimensional Priority Inversion Blocking (2D Blocking) under non-preemptive GEDF: one dimension is due to non- preemptivity, and the other dimension is due to parallelisminduced blocking where a job cannot execute if the number of idle processors is smaller than its degree of parallelism. This 2D blocking challenge may cause a gang job to be blocked for multiple times, and in the worst-case for an infinite number of times. Such a worst case scenario is actually seen in the example shown in Fig. 2, where τ 3,1 will be infinitely blocked by any subsequently released jobs due to the other six tasks in the system. Key intuition behind this analysis framework. The fundamental executing/non-executing interval analysis, which seeks to first categorize a task's (e.g. τ i 's) analysis interval into executing and non-executing subintervals and then characterize τ i 's execution behavior within each category, is provided in [1] to analyze the schedulability of preemptive gang task systems, but it cannot be applied to analyze non-preemptive gang task systems. The reason is that, after removing all lower-priority jobs from the non-preemptive schedule, during a non-executing interval of τ i , the number of idle processors may be greater than m i . This will ultimately cause the analysis impossible to upper bound the utilization loss due to such increased number of idle processors. Nonetheless, as proved in [1], this analysis framework is very effective in analyzing the gang parallelisminduced challenges under the preemptive case. Thus, our motivation is to invent new techniques, when combined with the executing/non-executing interval analysis framework, that could allow us to resolve both challenges due to nonpreemptivity and gang parallelism. Motivated by this, we propose a non-trivial "ghost job" generation method, which smartly generates a set of ghost jobs to occupy the idleness due to removing lower priority jobs in the non-preemptive GEDF schedule, thus allowing the beneficial properties of the executing/non-executing framework to hold even under the non-preemptive case.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis
div.p: We now present our developed schedulability analysis framework for analyzing non-preemptive gang tasks. Our approach is fundamentally based on the lag-based reasoning which has been used extensively to analyze ordinary sporadic task systems. We focus on analyzing what happens when a deadline is missed given a gang task system τ . Let t d denote the first time instant in any such schedule S at which a dead-line is missed. Let job τ i,j be the job that misses its deadline d i,j = t d and we focus on analyzing τ i,j and the time interval [0, t d ). We skip the description of the proof setup for lag-based reasoning herein, since the same description can be found in [1] (Sec. 4.1). We present our new ghost job generation method in Sec. 4.1, as well as the beneficial properties of the resulting schedules in Secs. 4.2 and 4.3, and finally derive a resulting schedulability test in Sec. 5.

div.head: Constructing a Ghost Schedule
div.p: Let job τ i,j be the job of interest that first misses its deadline d i,j = t d . As intuitively motivated earlier in Sec. 3, the key idea behind our new technique is the following: (i) we create a minimum set of ghost jobs (with specified release time, deadline, execution cost, and degree of parallelism), corresponding to the set of jobs with lower-priorities than τ i,j that execute within [0, t d ), (ii) we prove that if every job, including τ i,j , is schedulable under the resulting schedule S in which the original set of lower-priority jobs is removed from the schedule and the created set of ghost jobs is inserted into the schedule, then every job, including τ i,j , is also schedulable in the original schedule S, and (iii) we derive a utilization-based test for the constructed schedule S. Due to the second step, such a test also holds for the original gang task system. Let A i,j denote the time instant when τ i,j starts executing in S. We first remove τ i,j and all jobs with deadlines later than t d from S. Let J denote the set of removed jobs which start executing earlier than A i,j and have release times earlier than t d .

According to the release times of jobs in J, J can be further divided into two subsets: J e and J l . In J e , the release time of each job is earlier than r i,j ; in J l , the release time of each job is later than or equal to r i,j . Fact 1. Let τ h,l denote an arbitrary job in J and τ h,l = τ i,j . Let A h,l denote the time instant when τ h,l starts executing in S. Then, A h,l < A i,j .

We construct the new schedule S from S within [0, t d ), through removing jobs in J from S and adding ghost jobs into the resulting schedule (note that the ghost jobs are also scheduled under non-preemptive GEDF). We now explain our methods of generating the ghost jobs, depending on the two job subsets J e and J l . Note that we generate one ghost job corresponding to one job in J e or J l . Generating ghost jobs corresponding to the jobs in J e . Let τ p,q denote an arbitrary job in J e . According to the definition of J e , r p,q < r i,j and d p,q > t d . We generate a ghost job τ p,q with the following parameters: (i): the release time of τ p,q is r p,q ; (ii): the degree of parallelism of τ p,q is m p,q ; (iii): the execution time of τ p,q is e p,q ; (iv): the period of τ p,q is t dr p,q ; (v): the absolute deadline of τ p,q is t d . Let τ p denote the ghost task which only releases 1 job in S. Generating ghost jobs corresponding to the jobs in J l . Let τ x,y denote an arbitrary job in J l and e max denote the maxi-mal execution time of jobs in J l . According to the definition of J l , r x,y ≥ r i,j and d x,y > t d . We generate a ghost job τ x,y with the following parameters: (i): the release time of τ x,y is r i,j ; (ii): the degree of parallelism of τ x,y is m i ; (iii): the execution time of τ x,y is e max ; (iv): the period of τ x,y is p i ; (v): the absolute deadline of τ x,y is t d . Note that all ghost jobs in J l have the same release time, degree of parallelism, execution time, period, and absolute deadline. Since the problem job of interest τ i,j is in J l , we also create a corresponding ghost job. Let τ x denote the ghost task which only releases 1 job in S.

div.head: Inferring Schedulability in S through S
div.p: We now prove that if every ghost job including τ i,j is schedulable in S, then every corresponding job including the problem job of interest τ i,j must also be schedulable in S. The intuition behind the proof is straightforward: every ghost job including τ i,j has the same deadline at t d , which is no later than the deadline of the corresponding job in J. If we can prove that the completion time of each job in J in schedule S is no later than the completion time of the corresponding ghost job in J in schedule S, then every job in J including the problem job of interest τ i,j must also be schedulable in S because every ghost job including τ i,j is schedulable in S. Note that the execution time of each ghost job in J is no smaller than the execution time of the corresponding job in J and jobs execute non-preemptively in both S and S. We thus prove this claim through alternatively proving that the starting time of each ghost job in J in schedule S is no earlier than the corresponding job in J in schedule S.
Based on the methods for generating ghost jobs, the constructed ghost schedule S has the following properties.

Property 4. If the ghost task system τ is schedulable in S, then τ is schedulable in S.
Property 5. If the original task system τ is unschedulable in S, then the ghost task system τ in S is also unschedulable.

div.head: Bounding the Utilization due to Ghost Jobs
div.p: In this section, we first define and validate the PS schedule P S corresponding to the ghost schedule S. Then, we de-scribe the property associated with P S and bound the additional utilization due to ghost jobs, which enable us to derive a utilization-based test for S and thus S.

Similarly, a ghost PS schedule P S also exists corresponding to the ghost schedule S, where the additional ghost jobs will be performed with certain rates according to their defined execution time and period, and complete exactly at their defined deadlines in P S. The degree of parallelism for each task in τ s is smaller than m i and the degree of parallelism for each task in τ l is no smaller than m i . Let τ s+ = τ s ∪ {τ i }. Let K denote the number of tasks in τ s+ . Let e s+ max denote the largest execution time among tasks in τ s+ . Definition 5. According to the length of period of each task, the task set τ l (defined above) can be further divided into two subsets: τ l s and τ l l . The period of each task in τ l s is no greater than p i and the period of each task in τ l l is greater than p i . Lemma 1. Let τ p,q denote an arbitrary job in J e , then τ p / ∈ τ l s . Proof. According to the definition of J e , each job τ p,q in J e is released before r i,j and has a deadline later than t d . Thus, the period of τ p,q is larger than p i . Thus, we have τ p ∈ τ l l and τ p / ∈ τ l s . In order for our analysis to be correct, we have to ensure that a valid P S schedule exists. That is, we have to guarantee that the total utilization of τ is at most m at any time instant t in P S. This implies that the additional utilization due to all ghost jobs will not cause the total utilization of τ to exceed m. The following lemma gives a sufficient condition that provides such a guarantee through bounding the additional utilization due to all ghost jobs, denoted by U B . Definition 6. Let m(r q ) denote the parallelism of J(r q ), e(r q ) denote the execution time of J(r q ), and p(r q ) denote the period of J(r q ).

div.head: A Utilization-based Schedulability Test
div.p: In this section, we present our new lag-based analysis for GEDF-scheduled gang task systems by proving the following theorem based on Property 1 -5 and Property 6, which also leverages the GANG-specific executing/non-executing analysis framework proposed to analyze gang tasks under the preemptive scheduling scenario [1].
Theorem 1. GEDF correctly schedules any HRT implicitdeadline sporadic non-preemptive gang task system τ on M processors if
div.formula: U sum + U B ≤ (M + 1) × (1 - u i m i ) + 2u i -m i (2)
div.p: holds for all τ i ∈ τ , where
div.formula: U B = τx∈τ l l ( e x × m x p i -u x ) + K × e s+ max × m i p i . (3)

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we derive a utilization-based schedulability test for scheduling HRT sporadic gang tasks under nonpreemptive GEDF on multiprocessors. We invent a set of non-trivial techniques to characterize the pessimism due to the joint consideration of non-preemptivity and ganginduced parallelism in the analysis and a corresponding utilization-based schedulability test (first-of-its-kind) is derived.
